#3223. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3222. Xcode 27.3 adds GitHub Copilot to its built-in coding assistant

Apple released Xcode 27.3 beta 1 today with multiple new features, chief among them an expansion of its built-in coding assistant to support GitHub Copilot. Here are the details.

Since Xcode 26.3, developers have been able to integrate AI coding agents directly into Xcode, to help with tasks ranging from writing boilerplate code to updating entire projects based on their documentation, file structure, and more.

Apple initially introduced ChatGPT integration in Xcode 26, followed by Anthropic’s Claude. Then, in Xcode 26.3, the company expanded both integrations with agentic coding capabilities through OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Agent.

With Xcode 27, Apple added support for Google Gemini, alongside a redesigned interface, interactive planning, and multi-turn conversations.

Now, with Xcode 27.3, Apple is expanding the list of supported AI coding tools once again, this time adding GitHub Copilot.

The Xcode 27.3 beta 1 release notes include the following under the Coding Intelligence section:

As with the other agentic integrations, this is particularly good news for developers whose companies have standardized on GitHub Copilot, as they can now use their company’s preferred AI coding tool directly within Xcode.

Here are the full release notes for Xcode 27.3 beta 1:

Xcode 27.3 beta includes Swift 6.4 and SDKs for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, tvOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Xcode 27.3 beta supports on-device debugging in iOS 17 and later, tvOS 17 and later, watchOS 10 and later, and visionOS. Xcode 27.3 beta requires a Mac running macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later.

See Xcode Support to learn more about compatible platforms and deployment targets.

The company is currently executing a network optimization program to align production with shifting demand and reduce structural costs through plant idling and inventory management. Looking toward 2027, our preliminary outlook anticipates mid to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates pricing growth reflecting already communicated January 1 pricing actions for fixed based customers, fourth quarter 26 pricing actions on new quoted work, and the midyear pricing carryover across acquired businesses.

Since the acquired operations have lower average selling prices in our heritage business, acquisition mix will temper headline reported pricing growth in the first half of 27 particularly through May 15, the 1 year anniversary of the New Frontier Materials acquisition. We thus expect full year reported ASP growth in the mid single digit range. Importantly, these acquired operations provide meaningful opportunity for continued pricing growth over time as we apply our commercial practices across the expanded network. Turning to the end market trends, infrastructure remains our most resilient and aggregates intensive end market.

At the federal level, current surface transportation programs have been extended through December 11, 2026, while work continues toward a longer term extension and, ultimately, the next surface transportation authorization. We continue to see broad bipartisan support for infrastructure investment Importantly, 40% of the infrastructure investment in Jobs Act funding remains to be spent. Providing a multiyear runway for transportation investment. At the same time, state department of transportation budgets across many of our key markets remain at historically elevated levels. More than 60% of funding across our top states is derived from state and other nonfederal sources providing a more stable funding base.

Private construction presents a more mixed outlook with Dodge Construction Network forecasting nonresidential square footage starts of approximately 1.2 billion square feet in 2027 approximately 24% below the 2022 peak While interest rate sensitive private nonresidential construction remains soft, data centers, power generation, and warehouse development remain areas of relative strength. Data center project shipments more than doubled in the third quarter, versus the prior year's comparable period. Our extensive distribution network, particularly in Texas and Louisiana, positions us well to serve the scale and logistical complexity of these often geographically remote projects with both construction aggregates and lime for soil stabilization.

Power generation also represents a compelling longer term opportunity supported in part by the rapidly growing energy requirements associated with data centers and broader electrification. The US Energy Information Administration projections US electricity demand to increase 25% to 50% by 2050, requiring substantial additional generating capacity related infrastructure. Also encouraged by the ongoing recovery in warehouse construction building on the inflection that began in last year's third quarter. Recently reported investments, including Amazon's Project Mercury, which contemplates expanding its same day fulfillment network to more than 1 thousand facilities by 2031 underscore the longer term warehouse opportunity.

Infrastructure, together with data centers, power generation and warehouse account for approximately 50% of our aggregate shipments, providing meaningful exposure to end market supported by multiyear demand drivers. Cost of Goods Sold per ton, excluding external pass through freight increased 5.6%. Or 5.1% on an organic basis primarily reflecting higher cash costs, including diesel and other energy related expenses. Incremental depreciation, depletion and amortization expenses represented an additional $0.52 per ton. Excluding the diesel headwind, cost of goods sold per ton would have increased 3% or 2.6% on an organic basis reflecting disciplined controllable cost management by our operating teams. Most notably, organic labor cost per ton, our single largest cost category, declined modestly in the quarter and was roughly flat year to date.

Our specialties business delivered record quarterly revenues and cash gross profit of $362 million and $163 million respectively, LNA's $216 million revenue and $115 million cash gross profit contribution since the August 21 closing date further demonstrates the resilience of Lyme and the transaction's margin accretion to the enterprise. In a year characterized by significant acquisition and divestiture activity, related purchase accounting, and comparability impacts on reported results our record third quarter free cash flow of $426 million an increase of 18% demonstrates the strong underlying financial performance of the business. On a year to date basis, disciplined inventory management has unlocked $135 million while capital expenditures are $157 million lower than the prior year period.

These actions alone have contributed over $290 million of free cash flow improvement. Together with our strong year to date organic labor cost control, ongoing network optimization efforts, and other structural cost actions, we reaffirm our confidence in achieving $350 million incremental cash flow target discussed during the second quarter call. Turning now to our updated 2026 guidance and preliminary 2027 outlook. Our revised 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint of $2.48 billion includes expected contributions from LNA and reflects year to date performance. October shipment trends and an assumed normal winter. The outlook also incorporates continued inflationary pressure across diesel and other energy related cost categories, as well as New Frontier's impact on reported volume and headline pricing.

In 2027, we expect margin expansion driven primarily by mid- to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates pricing growth combined with ongoing network optimization disciplined cost management, and a full year contribution from LNA, we expect these benefits to more than offset continued inflationary pressure. Turning now to the balance sheet. We funded the cash consideration for the LNA transaction with a $1.5 billion pre-payable term loan and $5.5 billion of senior notes issued across several maturities with a weighted average coupon rate of approximately 5.5%. As discussed when announcing the transaction, we are committed to deleveraging to our targeted range of 2 to 2.5x net debt to adjusted EBITDA and retaining our investment grade credit ratings.

With deleveraging supported by the significantly enhanced free cash flow generation of the combined business. Ward, back to you.

Through portfolio optimization, we have built a more resilient and diversified business with increased contributions from our central division, and our higher margin specialties platform. At the same time, we are optimizing our aggregates network, and aligning production with current demand conditions, creating a leaner cost structure and a more efficient operating platform. Combined with the pricing discipline that has long been a hallmark of Martin Marietta, these actions position us to expand margins, while continuing to grow earnings and cash flow. So Ward, could you give us a little bit more detail on the puts and takes behind your preliminary 2027 pricing view of mid to high single digits, mix And what is your end market outlook? Could imply for organic aggregates volumes next year? And with this, maybe what your outlook is for the gross profit contribution from ags or cash gross profit contribution given your outlook for continued higher costs in 2027? Thank you.

C. Howard Nye: Trey, thanks for the question. Good morning to you. Trey, I will take you through several puts and takes on that. So let's start to your question with pricing. So currently, we see a nice path to mid to high single digit mix adjusted aggregates growth in 2027. And I think there is several reasons for that. Number 1, what we think we are going to see on January 1 price realization. I think that is important.

Number 2, what we are already seeing in quoting work that we are doing now in Q4 and on the 2027 projects that were coming next year, and then lastly, the carryover pricing on acquired volumes at the midyear price increases that we saw in the acquired businesses. As I indicated in the prepared remarks, those markets tend to be 50% or 25% below heritage Martin Marietta, So that is important that we got those in midyear. But equally gives us a nice track record going forward. What I will say relative to pricing, and I mentioned it briefly in the prepared remarks, cadence is gonna matter.

Because, obviously, as we anniversary both the Quikrete transaction in February and the New Frontier acquisition in May, you will see a nice bump those 2 anniversaries roll by. But keep in mind, if we are really thinking about the business in 2 different chunks, I would say this. The heritage business, about half of the shipments are fixed base and about half are quoted work. Again, if we are seeing nice quoted work pull through right now, I think that is important. Relative to the other part of your question with respect to volumes, I guess I would say several things. Number 1, the backlogs actually look very similar to what they did coming into this year.

I think that is a really good place to start. At the same time, as you and I discussed before, it is a dynamic market right now. So we are really just waiting to see the end of the year and have a much better feel on the precision of what volumes are going to look like. The thing that is important to remember relative to volume is we are gonna have a really tough Q1 compare. Because keep in mind, as we said last year, when Vale is having a bad winter, meaning they have no snow, we are having a great winter.

So keep in mind, the West and the central divisions came out of the box early in 2026 very, very aggressively. We do not anticipate that happening. Again, that goes back to Michael's comment. We are really looking for more normalized weather. With respect to the other part of your question on end market outlook, I would say several things. 1, think the best way to think about that is it continues to be relatively bifurcated.

And what I mean by that, residential and light nonres, simply remain pressured because of what is going on with interest rates and as we saw those rates move here in the second half of the year, we saw both of those hit a bit of an air pocket. Not a big surprise, You would have expected it. I expected it too. And, frankly, as long as mortgage rates remain above 7%, single family housing is just not gonna be in a terribly robust place. Now the converse of that is what we see going on in infrastructure and what we see in heavy non res.

So if we are looking at that, keep in mind those areas account for about half of our aggregates business. So when we are going into the new year with those performing well, I think that is important. So if we are looking at data centers, they remain an especially attractive opportunity. And what we are seeing is year over year, our data center volumes more than doubled year over year in the third quarter. And again, Texas is expected to represent approximately 30% of projected US data center capacity by 2028 And our leading position in Texas, not just in stone, but in lime today is gonna put us in a really attractive place for those multiyear projects.

But we have also discussed what is been happening relative to warehouse. We expect that recovery to continue. Again, if we are looking at warehouse and distribution construction, that is up approximately in our world by 51%. Year to date. And again, I mentioned what Amazon is doing between now and 2031, adding more than a thousand facilities. We think, again, that gives nice momentum going into the new year. And the last 1 I will mention, Trey, in response to your question, then I will ask Michael to come back and talk specifically about profit numbers that you have referenced. Is power generation.

And we are seeing that move in very considerable ways both relative to LNG and what is happening in portions of the Texas market, but more broadly, what is happening in data and data warehousing as well because we are seeing increasingly amounts of that going in behind the meter. So I have tried to give you a sense of what do I think is happening with price, what do I think is happening with volume, How are the end markets behaving that I think lead up to those? Then, Michael, I will ask you to come back and respond to the other portion of this question.

Michael J. Petro: Yeah, Trey, we will come back certainly with more specifics relative to our profit guide for next year. We are just given the preliminary pricing now. But as you know, pricing is the disproportionate lever for profit growth. And as Ward mentioned, we feel very confident about what we are going to be able to achieve January 1 there. So the mid to high single digits on a mix adjusted basis is definitely what you should be baking in. What I would tell you is inflation we expect continue.

Certainly with diesel where it is today, I think you can model a flat line there We are seeing all in with acquisitions about a $25 million headwind per quarter for diesel. So we will lap that in Q1 of next year. So we will have an incremental headwind going into next year in the first quarter until we start having same 1, same diesel comps. So think elevated inflation mid to high single digit pricing, and some of the commentary that Ward provided on volume out are able to get you to a preliminary profit number.

Operator: Our next question comes from Adam Thalhimer from Thompson Davis. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Adam Thalhimer: Hey. Good morning, guys. Nice job in a tough environment. Hey. Thanks. Can you update us on how the LNA integration is going? And why did they get off to such a fast start in Q3?

C. Howard Nye: Adam, thanks for the question. And look. that is obviously a bright spot in almost any circumstance. The integration is going just fine is the quick response. The work streams are well underway. The performance so far, to your point, has exceeded our initial expectations. The integration remains totally on track, so if you are really looking at what is happened in the 40 days since closing, cash gross profit was $115 million, adjusted EBITDA at $104 million, at 48-plus percent margin. And part of what I think people are now seeing is what we had long seen in that business and why we found it to be so compelling.

And keep in mind, we have not even started to get the additional contributions that we believe we are going to see as we continue to integrate this because we think the additional value creation that is going to come from cross selling in hot mix or Texas mega projects or otherwise is gonna be pretty considerable. So to your point, are we really remain focused on capturing those synergies just as quickly and thoughtfully as we can? We are. But here's the other piece that we are really focused on. it is a great business.

So the last thing that we want to do is do anything that takes a really good business, a high performing business, and puts it off track. The integration is going well. The synergy realization is going well. The cultures have come together. Actually very nicely. Their safety culture and ours aligned the way that we would hope Adam. So there is nothing that we are seeing in this that has been a negative surprise to us at all. And again, I think we will continue to have results that the street will see. And they will like and the merits of this transaction will simply become self evident. Thanks, Ward.

Operator: Thank you, Our next question comes from Kathryn Thompson from Thompson Research Group. Please go Hi.

Kathryn Thompson: Thank you for taking my question today. I appreciate your color on 2027 outlook and also for LNA. Congratulations again on closing that I think the next big subject are elections. So we wrapped up elections yesterday, and we are looking forward to hopefully, a reauthorization of the federal highway bill next year. Would like to get your thoughts in terms of how the elections may or may not impact this process. What you are seeing right now with states in terms of their spending and, you know, some of the inevitable things that happen such as holding up lettings, in advance of a highway bill? And are you seeing that in the states in which you operate? So much.

C. Howard Nye: Catherine, thanks so much. The question. I would say several things. 1, to your point, if we are really looking at states in the first instance and the fact that in our world, given the fact that we have tried to build our business in states that have really good fiscal conditions, The state budget circumstances matter disproportionately. And what we are seeing right now is very good, consistent, expected performance from the states. And what I mean by that is if I go in and look at. And states are important to us, which means now California, Texas, Georgia, Missouri, South Carolina, Colorado, Iowa, they are all maintaining or increasing transportation investment.

If we are looking at North Carolina and Florida, again, their funding is gonna be perfectly adequate for what we are looking to do next year. So as we are going into 2027, I do not see anything in the states that are disproportionately important to us that lead us to believe that there are gonna be any issues there. And to your point, have we seen any delay in lettings? The short answer is no. We have not. If we are looking on the other part of your question relative to what is going on from the federal level, Now keep in mind, when Build America 250 came out of the congress, it came out with 62-2 vote.

I mean, that tells us from the outset that this is a bipartisan bill. Look, do I think it is still possible that we could see something in a lame duck congress? Maybe. Do I think that is relatively unlikely? Probably. And do I think a democratic senate might push even harder relative to highways, bridges, roads, streets. And overall transportation? I think so. So long story short, do I think we should go ahead and plan for seeing probably a continuing resolution or 2 as the congress goes through that process. I think that is probably realistic. Is that something that concerns me? I would suggest to you frankly, not at all. Again, I think this is largely bipartisan.

I think we have got a group likely coming in who want to invest perhaps even more So, again, I am not seeing anything from the states that is concerning to me. I see a process going forward at the federal government, but I think we have seen before, and it is very navigable. The last thing that I would say, and I think this is important, if we go back and look at the last peak in aggregate shipments several years ago, You know what that was in the middle of? A continuing resolution.

And I think what happens is people oftentimes sit back, look at a CR, and wonder what is this going to mean for this very fundamental product that rolls out And the fact is, we simply go through these ebbs and flows, I think, in a very steady, very way. And I do not see anything at the federal level or the state level that makes me think otherwise, Catherine. So I hope that is responsive. that is very helpful. Thanks so much, and best of luck. Thanks, Katherine.

Operator: Our next question comes from Philip Ng from Jefferies. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Philip Ng: Hey, guys. I guess my question is for 2027 for either for Michael. If diesel prices and cost at these levels, is 3% to 4% cost per ton increase reasonable when we think about 2027? And then been really noisy this year. Outside of M&A, any callouts on mix and the loss or any noise in terms of that number as well? And I know they produce some construction grade aggregate as well. Yeah.

Michael J. Petro: No. Thanks, Philip, for the question. I think the short answer to your COGS per ton inflation estimate is probably in the general ZIP code. The best way to think about it for us on diesel is we will consume in the aggregates business all in with Quickrete and New Frontier. About 50 million gallons. You know, at current spot rates of about $4.70 a gallon. So that is gonna be the diesel comp that we will be looking at next year. And we are assuming planning purposes internally and for what we are doing relative to price, that type of diesel level for the for the balance of 2027. No, you were breaking up a little bit.

Philip Ng: Sure. From your from a mix standpoint for pricing, 2027, any callouts outside of M&A that could create some noise for 2027? Appreciate New Frontier and Quikrete and Lhoist, I believe they have some construction grade aggregates do not believe it is part of that equation, but does that have an impact in terms of we think about mix for 2027?

Michael J. Petro: Yep. No. So the Lhoist aggregates are certainly out of that. From a mix perspective in Q1, you will have the acquisition mix of New Frontier and 2 months of Quikrete. So on a reported basis, that will continue to be impacted by those tons flowing through. Of course, you get the benefit of the tonnage on volume in the Q1 comp on an as reported basis. Then in Q2, you have about 45 days of New Frontier.

So we begin to lap the acquisition comps midway through Q2 and that. that is generally speaking the mix from an acquisition perspective The other mix that we have had a lot of this year is the geographic mix on the organic business. That could very well turn into be a mix tailwind next year. As Ward mentioned, we do not expect we are expecting more of a normal winter. So we do not expect is for the central division and Colorado to come out of the gates with the volume growth that we saw those 2 divisions do. This year. So that means more contribution from the East and the Southwest, which tend to have higher average selling prices.

That said, that is why we are guiding preliminarily to a mix adjusted price metric of mid to high single digits. That would effectively capture all mix, whether it be organic and or acquisition.

C. Howard Nye: Hey, Let me come back and add 1 more thing too because the price conversation is really important. And thank you for the question. The other thing that I wanna make sure we do not drive by in this quote without talking about has been the cost performance of the business. Because I think our teams have done that in my view, extraordinarily well. So if we are looking at organic cost of goods sold, and I am going to exclude for these, external freight, it increased 5.1% of the quarter and 3.8% year-to-date. But excluding the diesel spike, and the corresponding increases were limited to 2.6% and 2.2%, respectively.

And 1 thing that I think is really important is if we are looking at labor cost per ton, which is our single largest cost category, that was flat for both the quarter and year to date. So I think your point's a good 1, and that is making sure you have your head around what is that pricing cadence next year. But keep in mind, the thing that we can really control within our gates is what is happening with respect to cost. And I like the setup relative to pricing, but I also like what I am already seeing relative to cost.

So forgive me for parachuting that in, Phil, but I think that is an important 1 to get Appreciate the color. Thank you, guys. You bet.

Operator: Our next question comes from Angel Castillo from Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Esther Osinaiya: Hi. This is Esther Osinaiya on for Angel Castillo. I just had a question on the aggregate sold to ready mixed customers. Is it mainly moved to April 1 increases. So do you see any changes in the ability to get price for ready mixed customers in 2027, like that timeline shifting to possibly twice a year versus that 1 time, April 1?

C. Howard Nye: Esther, thank you for the question. I would say several things. No. I do not. And what I think we are broadly seeing from ready mixed customers is as follows. I think some will be January 1, I think some will be April 1. I think there is just gonna be a primary difference in geographies. So think in geographies that are colder based, you will see April. I think in warmer based, you will see a January 1 price increase. And here's what we have heard very clearly from our concrete customers this year. It was very difficult for them given what was happening in private nonres and res markets to take a midyear price increase this year.

I think that is part of the pressure that you have seen this year. Their response has been I am seeing the same input issues you are. I know you are gonna have to go up in the New Year. Do this for me. Give me 1 price increase Hit me at the beginning of the year, and do not plan for midyear next year. I think that actually helps them in their planning. Frankly, from our perspective, moving that forward is very helpful as well. So I think your question relative to concrete is particularly well placed because I think that has been really 1 of the more challenging aspects of this year.

But, again, I think the answer is yes. We will see increases in some markets in January. Yes. We will see increases in some markets in April. We are gonna treat both of those relative to concrete as if that is going to be the only 1 during the course of the year. So, Esther, I hope that is helpful. Yes. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Anthony Pettinari from Citigroup. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Anthony Pettinari: Hey. So in the quarter, you saw ag's organic shipments decline and organic pricing up, I think, 2.7%. I am just wondering how that kind of compared with your expectations going into the quarter and if there were any factors in terms of weather? I mean, you talked about geographic mix. That you would call out when we look at 3Q and maybe think about 4Q.

C. Howard Nye: Yeah. I would I would say the primary thing that changed, Anthony, is number 1, the concrete guys could not take mid years this year. And just talk with Esther about that. So I think that is 1 thing. I do not see that persistent I think the other issue was, as interest rates moved. We simply saw the private work slowdown. And, again, not a big surprise. I think you have crossed the heavy side space.

I would be surprised if that is not a pretty consistent answer And part of what I think we are doing is we are looking at what happened with volumes because of that interest rate increase in September and then what we have seen in October. On a days affected basis. that is what is informed the way that we have looked at the balance of the year, particularly going into Q4. And again, last year, for example, we had a November that was a pretty heady November from a volume perspective. So, again, I think we are trying to just be very thoughtful. Maybe with a touch of conservatism. As we are looking at Q4 this year.

Okay. that is helpful. I will turn it over. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Keith Hughes from Truist. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Keith Hughes: Thank you. When you were talking about 2027, you called out the dates. So specifically anniversarying New Frontier. And I guess, Quikrete, in getting their prices up towards the Martin Marietta average. I assume you are not gonna get it all the way. Do you have any feel for how much of the gap between the 2 entities pricing you will be able to realize as we hit the second half of next year.

C. Howard Nye: Keith, that is a great question. So thank you for that. So I would say several things. 1, did we see mid years at the Quickrete operations New Frontier this year even though we closed New Frontier after the mid year? The answer is yes. We did. Do I anticipate that those will likely be marked in which we will look for mid years again next year? The answer is yes. I think we probably will.

Think to answer your question more directly, typically, what we have seen Keith, is probably a 36 month runway from the time that we buy a business until the time that we can get it closer to something that looks like a Martin Marietta average I do not think these are gonna be dramatically different. And 1 reason I would say that in many respects is the markets that are really hitting it the hardest right now tend to be those markets in the center part of the country. So if we are looking in markets in Missouri and Kansas City or others, those are markets that from a volume perspective have done very, very well this year.

And again, back to the notion on backlogs. Our backlogs in those markets also look attractive So I think I have given you A, where they sit today, b, the timeframe that we think we are likely to see that gap closed, and what I think will happen in those markets with mid years in 2027. You are welcome, Keith.

Operator: Our next question comes from Avi Jaroslawis from UBS. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Analyst: Good morning. So I know you are expecting positive price cost for the year next year, but should we expect that the organic price cost is going to turn positive early in 2027? Or should we continue to see some headwinds there for some time into next year? Maybe until we lap some of the, higher cost comps from this year?

Michael J. Petro: Yeah. No. We would think on an organic basis, so ex the reported mix impacts from the acquisitions, should see price cost out of the gate next year. Okay. Got it. And just quickly, maybe what are you expecting on that front for Q4? It look similar to Q3 or any differences? Yeah. So on an organic basis, for Q4, what we are seeing is implied in the guide is down high single digit volume. Up on a reported organic basis about 2% pricing. So that is a step up from the 1% that we saw in Q3. So we are starting to see a little bit of momentum from the quoting work flowing through.

But we expect to continue to have the elevated COGS inflation in Q4. So we think Q4 is certainly still price cost negative, the inflection point being what we are going to do on January 1. Okay. Very helpful. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jared Greenblatt from JPMorgan.

Garrett Samuel Greenblatt: Hi, thanks for taking my question. I just wanted to touch back on the Lhoist transaction and talk about some expectations between 2027 there. In terms of that, what is the cadence of when we should expect to see some of this cross selling volume start flowing through on the aggregate side? Maybe if you could talk about the timing of the royalty contracts you have. Then just on the price side of things, what are the dynamics or expectations you see for lime in 2027?

C. Howard Nye: Well, We will with the aggregate side in the fullness of time. I mean, those are contracts that are in place with companies that we and LNA have good relationships with, and we want to be very thoughtful. About those. If we start looking at really what we expect from LNA next year, part of what is going to be attractive about that business, we are anticipating about $820 million worth of EBITDA for 2027. And part of what is really appealing about that business is how steady we think that is going to look across the year.

And I think that is 1 of the things that we spoke up when we did the transaction because it adds such nice, stable, consistent predictable earnings. So if we think about what that is gonna look like, mean, this is pretty easy way to measure it. Probably 23% of profits will come through in Q1, 27%-ish in Q2, 27% in Q3, and then back to 23% in Q4. So really, you have got it bookended with 23%. You got 27% in the middle, which means you are getting about a 50/50 split. During the course of the year.

I think to the other part of your question, we are already having our sales teams working very collaboratively looking at either DOT jobs, data center jobs, etcetera. Because keep in mind, part of what is going to happen now on either Public Works or big heavy private nonres works is we can look at those jobs together. And in some instances, they are gonna want base stone, clean stone, etcetera. In other instances, they may want the lime, particularly as they are working through in some respects, unsuitable or challenging soils. Or in some instances, we may want to push them 1 way or another for various reasons that are to the customer's benefit.

So you will clearly see the benefits of cross selling coming through as we get into 2027. Frankly, I think we will start seeing some of that even here in the latter part of 2026. Again, I hope that answered your question.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ivan Yi from Wolfe Research. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Ivan Yi: Yes. Good morning, guys. Thanks for the time. You bet. You did not break out you did not break out specific the volumes and the pricing for the lime business, but can you speak directionally about how LNA tonnage and pricing trended in 3Q? And also, what are you seeing thus far in 4Q? Thank you.

Michael J. Petro: Yeah. No. We are we are still looking at ultimately what is gonna be the level of disclosure for specialties business as we balance providing appropriate visibility so that the investing community can make informed decisions versus disclosing anything competitively sensitive. So I think it is all part of the evaluation that we are taking a look at. But what I can say on volume and price just on a percentage basis, both were up nicely with revenue in the period that we ended in September was up about double digits. And I would say the trend in October on 1 less shipping day looked similar. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael Dudas from Vertical Research.

Michael Dudas: Good morning, Jacklyn. Michael, and Ward. Good morning. Maybe this 1 for Michael. You highlighted some positive operating and free cash flow metrics in the quarter and your outlook for the year. Maybe you can early look on 2027 on CapEx, or can you continue to get some working capital tailwinds as we move to 2027? And, you know, looking at relative to what free cash flow generation could be versus what you had thought coming into the Lhoist acquisition?

Michael J. Petro: How's it played through? Yes. So the Lhoist business, as you know, is just a cash generation machine because it does not require a lot of CapEx given back to a question that we were talking about earlier. They largely outsource a lot of the mining. So crushing rock, it wears down crushers, conveyors, equipment, etcetera, is on a third party's dime. So extremely good cash flow conversion from EBITDA generated from LNA given the limited CapEx requirements.

C. Howard Nye: But I would say for next year, our CapEx guide when we do come out with it will include CapEx all in inclusive of acquisitions. But we still expect that to be within that guide that we provided at the Capital Markets Day, which would suggest about 25% of EBITDA. So we do not see any difference in that. Relative to working capital, we are getting a lot of the benefits this year. In terms of working capital inflows relative to inventory. What we are gonna look to do is stabilize that so that we do not have it swinging the other way into a working capital outflow. Moving forward.

So I would not expect the same quantum of cash flow impact as a result of inventory management, but I would not expect it to reverse and go the other way.

Michael Dudas: And we are looking at some tuck in acquisitions you made. You now close of 1 in September. How does that play out the next 12, 18 months given the deleveraging focus on top of what this. I am sure it is pretty interesting pipeline still for additions for your business.

C. Howard Nye: It is. And, Michael, thank you for the question on that. Actually, the way that we structured the transaction between cash and equity, was very purposeful because we did not want to have ourselves on the sidelines if we saw. If attractive bolt on acquisitions. Now that said, the delevering process is going to be important. And we are going to start that here in the fourth quarter with approximately $500 million of debt repayment coming up over the coming weeks. So I think you will see a nice blend. Will we invest in the business, to Michael's point, from a CapEx perspective? That we think is appropriate Absolutely. Will we be paying down debt? To be sure.

And will we continue to be in the bolt on business in. On the aggregate Just as you saw with the Fraser transaction that was announced, we will continue to do that and we have the ability to do it. So you for the question. Thank you, guys.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brent Thielman from Oppenheimer. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Brent Thielman: Hey, thanks. Good morning. Ward, maybe just on LNA, it looks like you were low 40% gross margin ex the markup on a shortened quarter. Can you just talk about your ability to protect those margins? Or even expand on those margins in a kind of a dynamic cost environment.

C. Howard Nye: You know, the nice thing about that business is, you know, a big piece of their cost is energy. They have looked at that from a very different lens than we have historically in aggregates. We looked at it 2 degree in this dimension in cement because there is some hedging that goes on with that. So again, it tends to be very, very predictable. The pricing in that space tends to be pretty constructive as new work comes up. And keep in mind, the other thing that is different about that business is in many respects, we have got contracts going forward that we know are in place that have built in inflators in them.

So, again, it is a business that we talked about before from quarter to quarter, from a year to year, and otherwise, you can actually model really very, very well. And yeah, I think having the business positioned in the Southern of the United States where we continue to see remanufacturing, where we continue to see significant energy work. Whereas I indicated in my prepared remarks, Texas is gonna have 30% of the data center activity over the coming years. We see something in that business that we believe is highly durable and highly resilient, and that was 1 of the reasons that we were so attracted to it. Frankly, for the last decade.

And, again, we have we have been watching that space. And keep in mind, even if you look at our heritage Woodville plant, I mean, that was the business that was seeing nice growth at the mid sing. Mid single digits range for 20 years. And again, we love that business. But where that sits geographically does not have the same dynamism that the Lhoist business that we have acquired, Donald.

So I think when we look at the history of the Lyme business that we have had, and how durable that margin has been, and then what this new business looks like in a more southern climate and importantly, what those businesses can now do together under 1 roof I think that leads us, Brent, to the overall durability of what we have. So I do not look at that. And lose any sleep over it in any respect. Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from David MacGregor from Longbow Research.

David MacGregor: Yes. Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. Kind of late in the call here, but I wanted to just tap your thoughts on the M&A market. And you have responded a little bit to this to Michael's question earlier. But I am just wondering to what extent you are seeing valuations maybe being impacted by higher rates and narrower price cost performances. Cost inflation. What are you seeing from sellers right now?

C. Howard Nye: You know, it is interesting. My view has long been that once sellers determine what they think their business is worth, they usually reside there for an extended period of time. So I am not seeing a lot of degrees change in that right now. It may mean something on how receptive the market is to it in some respects, David. But I have not seen any notable change. The other thing that happens is on occasion in those circumstances, rather than having a change in value, They just have a change in timing. So again, from my perspective, I do not see a change in the way sellers are thinking about value.

We may see a degree of what they are thinking and timing. And all of that is fine. We are playing this in a very long ball fashion. And we want to grow our business really responsibly. I think we have and our track record indicates that, and I think we will continue to do so. But I hope that helps, David. It does. Thanks, Ward. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brian Brophy from Stifel. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Brian Brophy: Yes, thanks. Good morning, everybody. Appreciate taking the question. Just a follow-up on the 2027 pricing discussion. Obviously, the cost outlook remains pretty fluid here. If we see any diesel inflation or inflation, between now and near year end, to what extent does that change the outlook for January 1 price increases just given the timing of pricing letters and customer discussions? Thanks.

C. Howard Nye: Brian, it is a great question. I would say probably several things. 1, I think what changes in a more immediate circumstance is what overall bidding looks like. So keep in mind, about half of it is gonna be fixed base, half of it is gonna be some form of bidding, And with the PreciseIQ tool that we have, part of what we are able to do is move that algorithm very, very quickly to make sure that we are taking into account what we are seeing change in the marketplace. So to your point, we recognize this dynamic Yes. Do our customers recognize this dynamic? The answer to that is yes as well.

And have we put in tools in the last 18 months that in my view allow us to navigate that with even greater agility going into 2027. To be sure we have. So I think that is how we see that playing out, Brian. Appreciate it. Very helpful. You bet.

#3217. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3216. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

If a school doesn't want AI in search, it doesn't get search at all

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each school can do what it wants when it comes to restricting or banning AI. However, a new report from The New York Times report found that schools that completely ban AI will also lose access to Google Search, one of the most ubiquitous tools on the internet for finding, well, anything.

"Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. He also explained that students "will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available."

Getting through college without access to Google sounds difficult, since almost everyone goes there when they need to learn something. Sure, Google alternatives exist, but for most people, an online search is still called "Googling."

As you might expect, Google's stance has drawn pushback. Lina Khan, former chair of the FTC, said to the NYT that Google is using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its AI.

Obviously, Google is justifying this move by saying that AI is an integrated part of search as it stands now. And that might be true, but we had many, many years of Google Search without AI, so it's certainly possible to find content on the web without it.

"This latest move shows it remains unchastened. As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools," Khan added. "Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line."

Two options for search inside school-issued accounts will launch in early 2027.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The first option will be search with AI overviews and AI chats, similar to the experience we use every day. The other will be search with Guided Learning, the student feature within Google’s Gemini chatbot. This feature is meant to guide students step-by-step without just giving them the answers. It is supposed to offer an experience similar to one-on-one tutoring.

Either way, we know it's possible to use search without AI, and if Google really wanted to, it could almost certainly allow schools to keep using its search engine without AI. We did it for years.

Will Google stick to its guns here, or will the company back down if there's enough backlash? After all, Google makes a lot of its money from search ads, and if It suddenly lost millions of students, that could hurt the bottom line over time.
