We have included reconciliations between Non-GAAP financial information and its GAAP equivalent in the press release and presentation materials. Today's call is copyrighted by the Timken Company, and without express written consent, we prohibit any use, recording, or transmission of any portion of the call. With that, I would like to thank you for your interest in the Timken Company, and I will now turn the call over to Lucian.

Lucian Boldea: Thanks, Neil, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us today to discuss our quarterly results and outlook. I would like to begin by thanking our Timken team for their dedication to our customers and for the significant progress they have made in advancing our company's transformation. As I reflect on my first year at Timken, I am proud of what we have accomplished together. We have developed and deployed our Elevate to Outperform strategy to build upon our strong foundation and transform Timken into a leader in advanced motion technology.

We have aligned our teams around our disciplined execution framework that anchors the strategy and made substantial progress towards achieving our 2028 targets, most notably in Industrial Motion, where we delivered high single-digit organic sales growth and significant margin expansion so far this year. The steps we have taken and early results reinforce my confidence in our direction and the significant opportunities ahead. Let me now turn to our third quarter performance, including the advancements we are making in executing our strategic priorities. In the quarter, total sales were up 4.7% versus last year, and organic revenue grew by nearly 3%, driven by positive pricing and higher volumes in the Industrial Motion segment.

We saw improving demand trends across most of our industrial markets, and if you exclude the significant decline in China wind energy sales from a very strong third quarter in 2025, organic sales were up mid-single digits from last year. We expanded EBITDA margins to 18.5%, driven by positive price cost and higher volumes. Adjusted earnings per share increased 20% year over year to $1.65. We also generated over $228 million in free cash flow. Regarding capital allocation, we repurchased more than 500,000 shares during the third quarter, substantially increasing our buyback activity from the first half of the year. Our net leverage ratio also declined to 1.7x EBITDA.

Our strong balance sheet gives us flexibility to fuel our capital allocation priorities. In the quarter, we delivered meaningful progress across all three pillars of our strategy as we put 80/20 and our disciplined execution framework to work across the entire enterprise. Starting with pillar one, optimizing the portfolio, we completed the divestiture of the belts business near the end of the quarter. This is an important milestone in achieving our 2028 financial targets, and we expect this action to increase Industrial Motion EBITDA margins by more than 200 basis points in 2027. We also continue to build great momentum with 80/20.

With employee training largely complete and work streams established and underway, 80/20 teams are taking actions across our businesses and regions. A few recent examples include the implementation of minimum order values for customers to reduce our cost to serve and improve profitability without negatively impacting total revenue. We also established our differentiated commercial service model to drive incremental growth with our 80s customers. Key account playbooks have been developed and deployed at a number of large accounts to grow our share of wallet by engaging as a One Timken solution provider. Overall, I am very encouraged by what we are seeing.

These initiatives are well underway and generating positive early results by reducing complexity and expanding margins while increasing our focus on the fastest-growing customers and verticals. That brings us to pillar two, where we are stepping up our resources, investments, and customer-facing efforts to drive outgrowth within our strategic verticals. Building a vertically aligned M&A pipeline is also a priority. This organizational focus contributed to double-digit growth in automation and robotics during the quarter. We also completed a minority investment in an early-stage manufacturer of electroadhesive technology, highlighting how we're expanding our technology model to align with next-generation motion technology. This investment is intended to support our growth in automation and robotics.

For pillar three, our One Timken operating model is fully in place to speed up decision-making and execution, and to bring together commercial and operating organizations. Our recently announced chief commercial officer structure is connecting strategic marketing, sales excellence, and execution across our multinational footprint to generate greater differentiation, enhance customer value, and most importantly, accelerate growth. This supports our One Timken commercial strategy, which is already driving greater integration across many of our platforms, including precision drive. For example, in precision drive, Cone Drive and Spinea brought together complementary technologies and expertise to develop an integrated actuator solution for the commercial space industry. It is an exciting example of our evolution towards a system-based solution.

We're also accelerating the integration of our lubrication systems platform. Over the past decade, we have added capabilities in this space through strategic acquisitions. Today, we are reducing portfolio complexity, aligning commercial resources with our strategic verticals, and aggressively scaling across Timken's multinational footprint beyond the business's largely European base. Our chief operating officer structure, led by Steve Ribaudo, who joined Timken in September, is now responsible for our P&Ls. With this structure, business leaders have greater accountability for the strategic choices that shape business performance, investment, and long-term competitiveness.

Additionally, by bringing the entire supply chain footprint under a single organization and aligning individual factories with P&Ls, we will continue to benefit from right-sizing and maintaining a nimble and globally flexible footprint that is competitive on cost and lead times to support our customers' growth. Taken together, these actions show how the Timken team is moving with speed to execute our Elevate to Outperform strategy. We are focused on finishing the year strong and delivering our 2026 outlook, and we are confident in our ability to achieve even stronger performance next year.

While it is still early, we currently expect our organic sales to increase by mid-single digits during 2027, driven by incremental growth from our strategic initiatives and further positive momentum across our industrial markets. As one example of the momentum we are seeing, the company's backlog at the end of the third quarter grew sequentially and was up mid-single digits from last year. With that, let me turn the call over to Mike for a more detailed review of the results and outlook. Mike?

Mike Discenza: Thanks, Lucian, and good morning, everyone. For the financial review, I am going to start on slide six of the materials with a summary of our third quarter results. Overall, total revenue for the quarter was $1.21 billion, which was up 4.7% from last year. Adjusted EBITDA margins increased to 18.5%, and adjusted earnings per share for the quarter was $1.65. Note that our adjusted results include a net benefit for IEEPA tariff refunds of approximately $12 million, or $0.13 per share. Turning to slide seven, let's take a closer look at our third quarter sales. Organically, sales were up 2.8% from last year.

The increase was driven by higher volumes in the Industrial Motion segment and positive pricing across both segments. Looking at the rest of the revenue walk, the acquisition of Bijur Delimon added 1.8% to sales in the quarter, while foreign currency translation had minimal impact on the top line. On the right, you can see third quarter performance in terms of organic growth by region. In the Americas, our largest region, we were up 6%, driven by growth across both segments and most end market sectors. In EMEA, we were down 3% from last year, driven by lower demand in the Engineered Bearings segment, while Industrial Motion revenue was relatively flat with last year.

Finally, we were up 3% in Asia Pacific, driven primarily by strong growth across most of the region, partially offset by lower sales in China. Turning to slide eight, adjusted EBITDA was $225 million, or 18.5% of sales in the third quarter, compared to 17.4% of sales last year. Let me comment a little further on a few of the different drivers on the EBITDA bridge you can see on this slide. Starting with the impact of pricing in the quarter, it was positive $12 million and added 1% to the top line, as we continued to benefit from pricing actions over the last year.

As you can see on the slide, tariffs had a $14 million net favorable impact versus last year, driven by the benefit of refunds and modestly lower tariff costs compared to the prior year. Looking at material and logistics, costs were modestly higher versus last year, driven by logistics. With respect to the manufacturing cost line, the increase primarily reflects labor and other cost inflation, including investments we are making to strengthen our aerospace and defense operations. Moving to the SG&A and other line, expenses were up from last year, as expected, driven primarily by higher compensation expense and spending on strategic initiatives.

Finally, our Bijur Delimon acquisition contributed $4 million to adjusted EBITDA in the quarter, with a high teens margin. Now let's move to our business segment results, starting with Engineered Bearings on slide nine. Engineered Bearings sales were $771 million in the quarter, up 0.7% from last year. Organic sales were up 0.5%, driven by higher pricing, while volumes were relatively flat. Among market sectors, aerospace and defense achieved the strongest gain versus last year. We also posted growth across the automation and industrial solutions, infrastructure, and industrial transportation and mobility sectors. However, we experienced a double-digit decline in power and electrification, driven by a significant decrease in China wind revenue.

Note that organic sales for the segment were up more than 3% from last year, when excluding the impact from China wind. Engineered Bearings adjusted EBITDA was $156 million, or 20.2% of sales in the third quarter, compared to 18.8% of sales last year. Margins in the quarter benefited from tariff refunds and favorable price mix. However, margins were negatively impacted by higher operating costs compared to last year. Now let's turn to Industrial Motion on slide 10. Industrial Motion sales were $440 million in the quarter, up 12.4% from last year. Organically, sales increased 7.3%, driven by higher demand across most market sectors and higher pricing.

The Bijur Delimon acquisition also added more than 5% to the segment's top line in the quarter. Among market sectors, A&D was up nearly 20% versus the prior year. We also generated growth across automation and industrial solutions, infrastructure, and power and electrification, while industrial transportation and mobility was relatively flat with last year. The segment saw solid growth in the quarter across all product platforms and was led by double-digit gains in linear motion systems. Industrial Motion's adjusted EBITDA margins came in at 19.8% of sales in the third quarter, up 80 basis points from last year. The increase in segment margins reflects the impact of higher volumes and favorable price mix. Organically, segment incremental margins were about 30%.

Moving to slide 11, you can see that we generated operating cash flow of $256 million in the third quarter, and after CapEx, free cash flow was $221 million, up significantly from the prior year. From a capital allocation standpoint, we returned $89 million of cash to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends in the third quarter. Note that we have approximately 9 million shares remaining on our repurchase authorization. Looking at the balance sheet, we ended the third quarter with net debt to adjusted EBITDA at 1.7x, which is an improvement from last quarter, driven by higher EBITDA and debt paydown. Now let's turn to the current outlook for full year 2026 with a summary on slide 13.

Starting with the bottom line, we are increasing our adjusted earnings per share outlook to the range of $6.35-$6.50, which represents 20% growth at the midpoint versus 2025. With respect to net sales, we expect total revenue to increase approximately 5.5%, unchanged versus the midpoint of the prior range. Organically, we are reaffirming our outlook for revenue to be up 3.5% at the midpoint. Currency translation is estimated to contribute around 1.25% to sales for the year, up slightly from the prior guide. M&A is expected to add 0.75% to full-year revenue on a net basis. The Bijur Delimon acquisition continues to perform well, while the updated outlook now reflects the impact of the belts divestiture on the fourth quarter.

The current earnings outlook implies that our 2026 consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin will be in the mid-18% range at the midpoint, slightly higher than the prior guidance, to primarily reflect the third-quarter performance. Moving to free cash flow, we expect to generate $375 million-$400 million in 2026, unchanged from the prior outlook. On slide 14, we provide an updated view on our 2026 organic sales outlook by end market sector, which includes the impact of both volumes and pricing. Again, we are reaffirming the full-year organic sales growth rate of 3.5%. You can see that we upgraded our outlook for the automation and industrial solutions sector, while we reduced our outlook for the power and electrification sector.

Note that our outlook assumes that sales in the China wind market decline again in the fourth quarter, both sequentially and year-over-year. Keep in mind that our China wind business is expected to be only a low single-digit percentage of total company sales in 2026, with the run rate in the second half of this year now below prior trough levels. As a result, we would not expect this business to have a significant impact on the full-year 2027 outlook, and supports the step-up in the organic sales outlook for next year that Lucian highlighted earlier. Moving to slide 15, here we provide a bridge of the increase in our 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook at the midpoint.

Most of the increase is driven primarily by our outperformance in the third quarter, including the impact of the tariff refunds. You can also see that we are adding $0.08 per share to reflect a lower net interest expense outlook for the year compared to our last guide. In summary, Timken delivered solid results in the third quarter, including double-digit earnings growth and strong cash flow. We have a strong balance sheet, significant capital deployment optionality, and are well-positioned to achieve strong earnings growth again in 2027. Let me turn it back over to Lucian for some final remarks before we open the line for questions. Lucian?

Lucian Boldea: Thanks, Mike. Let me reiterate that we are focused on delivering a strong finish to the year while making continued progress on our Elevate to Outperform strategy, which is a multi-year transformation. In 2026, we have taken significant actions to transform the core of our business, to reduce complexity and exit non-strategic underperforming businesses, refocus our resources on strategic verticals, and integrate our Timken operating system. As a leadership team, we take our commitments very seriously and will continue to work relentlessly to deliver what we committed to. Our plans are on track, and we remain confident that our strategy will accelerate growth, structurally increase margin, and drive significant shareholder value over the coming years.

Mike Discenza: Thanks, Lucian. This concludes our formal remarks. We will now open up the line for questions. Operator?

Operator: Gentlemen, thank you. To our phone audience joining today, at this time, we will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, you may press star and then the digit one on your telephone. If you are using a speakerphone today, please pick up your handset prior to pressing the keys. If you would like to withdraw your question, repeat the steps. Star one will also remove you from the queue. We will take just a moment to pause momentarily while we assemble our roster. First, from the line of Bryan Blair with Oppenheimer.

Bryan Blair: Thank you. Good morning, guys.

Bryan Blair: We know your Q4 organic sales outlook is unchanged, similar growth to Q3. Maybe offer a little more color on how orders trended through October and how we should think about core growth by segment in the fourth quarter. I assume that China wind is a little bit less of a, quote-unquote, "bad guy" on the Engineered Bearings side, and the comp is obviously a bit healthier for Industrial Motion.

Lucian Boldea: Thank you, Bryan. I think when you look at you have to look at the context of Q3 and Q4 in everything that we're doing to transform the company. You're a little bit looking at not going across the water and not everything that's happening beneath the surface. We're definitely focusing our resources where we said, and you look at the early wins, we alluded to that in our prepared remarks, where our pipeline sat year-over-year. Our pipeline is up in Q3, mid-single digit. What's more exciting is the percent increases that happen in that pipeline in our focus verticals. Whether you're talking about automation and robotics, or we're talking about aerospace and defense, where there are significant double-digit increases.

Those happen in Q3 in the pipeline. Obviously, they will continue to happen. We expect for them to continue to happen in Q4 as well. The demand picture externally, we don't see that being dramatically different going from Q3 to Q4. The undercurrent from all this is also, obviously, we have an automotive OE unwind that is already having a little bit of volume impact that we're offsetting with growth. There's a lot of churn in here that we're doing to really deliver on a number and on a commitment that we have made.

I'm proud of the team that we have done that, and we're trying to give that same kind of appropriate guidance for Q4 on what we believe we're going to do. The pipeline order book that we're looking at, all the indicators say that we're headed in the right direction. It is going as planned. There are no big surprises. Assuming the market just holds the way it is and continues to stay where it is, then we feel very good about our ability to deliver similar performance in Q4. We've already given a little bit of a view into 2027 without really giving a guide, but that's where we are.

Bryan Blair: I appreciate the color. You did offer a segue to the preliminary 2027 outlook there, so have to dive in a bit. Is it fair to assume that, consistent with the medium-term framework you've put out there and performance through 2026, that you're contemplating high single-digit Industrial Motion growth next year, more low single on the bearings side? If we look across your major end markets, I think you alluded to some of these dynamics in your prior answer, but how would you rank order growth expectations given current visibility?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, absolutely. I think if you look, I think what you said is appropriate. Obviously, now we focus on finishing 2026 strong, but the destiny for Q1 is pretty much set during Q4, so we definitely are focusing on both. I think it's a little early to comment on 2027 with a lot of certainty, but expecting organic sales to increase by mid-single digits is still the case. Our strategic initiatives are starting to drive incremental growth, and those will, of course, only accelerate as we move forward. The markets that you were asking about, absolutely, automation and robotics is very much the leader in driving that growth, but right behind it is A&D.

In both of these, we're seeing increases in our pipeline of double digit year-over-year, and it's not a low double digit number. It's a very healthy double digit number. That gives us a lot of confidence that we will be able to start benefiting more and more from pivoting that portfolio. Obviously, there's still pricing. I'm sure there'll be other questions on pricing later, but to tease that a little bit early on, our price minus cost in Q3 was positive on a year-over-year basis. It was positive sequentially. We expect the same in Q4, both year-over-year as well as sequentially from Q3. So, that says that our discipline around pricing is there.

Our track record is now there, so we feel good about that being additive to our organic, to our volume growth going into 2027. There's 80/20, obviously, that's going to start being a beneficiary not only to the bottom line, but to the top line as we focus on customers. So, that will help as well. On the margin side, belts, you're going to start seeing that already in Q4, and really we feel good about seeing a significant impact to that in 2027. We've committed to more than 200 basis points of Industrial Motion margins, so that's a third of the company. So, take a third of that number, 60 to 70 basis points from the belts.

So, again, all those actions that we have taken without really providing a formal outlook make us confident in our ability to achieve stronger performance in 2027 as we continue to build upon what we're executing today.

Bryan Blair: Understood. Thank you again.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of David Raso at Evercore.

David Raso: Hi, thank you for the time. I was curious, you spoke of auto OE exits as part of the fourth quarter comments, but when you speak of organic sales next year, mid-single digit growth, is that including with some of the auto exits or excluding? Just to level set, and I have a follow-up.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, what we've committed to is a net number. Absolutely. Yes.

David Raso: Okay, so the mid-single digit is even with, and I'll put a number around it, $100 million of revenue backed away from an auto. Even with exiting that, you still look at mid-single digit. It includes the exiting, just to be clear.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, I'll remind you that the exit is, the majority of the revenue exit is not in 2027. That happens in 2028. But there is a number in 2027 as well. It's smaller than what you mentioned. It's a part of the total, but the majority is in 2028. But yes, the number is a net number, is the answer.

David Raso: Okay, helpful. Because I'm just trying to understand. I thought the China wind business, the comp gets easier in the fourth quarter to the extent where EB this quarter would have been like 3.8% organic without the China wind drag. That's why I'm just curious if that's sort of the bogey and the wind year-over-year. If I remember correctly, it's not much of a decline. If you kept it, like China wind, I guess sequentially, are we now kind of flat-lining a little bit sequentially? Because if that's the case, I think the comp becomes almost nil.

David Raso: Why would EB go from 3.8% ex-wind to still sub three in the fourth quarter? I'm just trying to get the confidence on EB showing any growth into 2027, and why is that a credible view?

Lucian Boldea: Right. No, that's very fair. Again, we can go into more detail on China wind, but what I would tell you is at a high level, there is another step down sequentially going from Q3 to Q4. But when you look at it at that point, it really becomes low single digit percentage of the total, so it's no longer that significant. Having said that, if you'll recall first half of 2026, we had pretty strong performance. It was also in the back half of 2025, so there was about a 12-month period that was pretty strong.

China wind tends to be a little more cyclical, a little more lumpy, and there's nothing that says that overall demand is going away or that we're not competitive or any of that. What the reality of that market is, it does tend to be a little more cyclical, and so we're now in the down cycle. But yeah, it's a little bit down. Q4 versus Q3 is another step down sequentially.

David Raso: And one last thing, sorry if I missed it. The mix issue that hurt the. When I do price cost, I also include the mix in it, and that mix was the real drag when we look at price cost. I am excluding IEEPA. The mix was very different in this quarter. It was a negative two, and last quarter, I think it was a positive $13 million. Did I miss it? What was the big mix change?

Mike Discenza: No, you are right, David. You did not miss it. It was primarily in the Industrial Motion segment where we had the larger mix impact, and it really is just the shift in where the growth was. So, we grew still in some of the higher margin businesses, but grew at a slower rate in the higher margin businesses and a little bit faster in some of the lower margin businesses. So, it really was just a mix. And think, the highest margin businesses, lubrication, linear motion, et cetera, are Philadelphia Gear business, and then lower margin businesses like chain and some of the more OE-focused markets.

So, it really was just a shift between the markets and the growth rates between the quarters.

David Raso: Thank you. I appreciate the time. Oh, sorry, again, Lucian.

Lucian Boldea: Thank you. No, and I was also going to add regionally, I think if you look at where our slow growth was, Industrial Motion has a very heavy European footprint, Europe being down in Q3, and really almost all of that happened in the month of August. That also weighed down that mix from a regional standpoint.

Operator: Our next question will come from Angel Castillo at Morgan Stanley.

Oliver: Hey, good morning, guys. This is Oliver on for Angel today. Maybe just

Oliver: when we look across. Good morning. When we look across kind of organic growth across your peers, I mean, do you feel like you have a mandate to go and take more price? Or maybe are we making some sort of strategic choice here in terms of price cost? I mean, just hoping you could help us understand kind of confidence in re-acceleration going forward.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, really appreciate the question. As I said, we're in the midst of a pretty significant transformation on how we're thinking about our business, how we're. On one hand, yes, you think of the three pillars of the strategy and how we're trying to focus on the right verticals. We're doing 80/20 to focus on our 80s customers to get more share of wallet, to be a little bit less cyclical than we are today, and to really be more resilient and more efficient in our growth. We've also started now to do is we set up a Chief Operating Officer organization, and we're frankly looking at our assets differently.

We are taking that sweat the assets mindset, which means leveraging that fixed cost. It's a two-step process. We look in the mirror, we look at our cost structure, we build a competitive cost structure, and then with confidence, we go out and compete, and we use the capacity that we have. When the capacity is not competitive, then we take action and we reduce that capacity. But it's our job to maintain the capacity that's competitive, then once we have it, we use it.

Aligning those P&Ls with the factories and really having that sweat the asset focus is going to get additional opportunity to do some of the things that you are talking about, especially on the Engineered Bearings side, where you're more fixed cost intensive, and so that fixed cost leverage does create a lot of value.

Oliver: Understood. Maybe just to follow up on that, I mean, One Timken, it's helped you drive some early wins here. You're able to combine some different capabilities. I mean, the question is the sum greater than the parts here? Is there some margin uplift or maybe some revenue uplift that's maybe we're not fully appreciating?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, the sum is much greater than the parts, and the sum is greater than the parts both in how we operate, but also how we present ourselves to the market. One Timken sometimes is a big word, and people take it to the extreme that it means every product line to every customer. Clearly, it doesn't. But if you look at data in any pick-the-random company, what you will find is if you take one customer that does business with three or more business units inside a company, that customer is more loyal, that customer is more sticky, you have more ability to collaborate with that customer in innovation.

It's just everything gets better with a multi-business line customer. And that doesn't happen if you leave it kind of to one business at a time, everybody for themselves. If you present yourself to that customer as one company, then you can combine the appropriate value, the appropriate offerings, so that the sum of the parts is greater. It also allows you to bring more of a solution in. We used the example in the prepared remarks where we were talking to somebody in the space industry, and they were an existing customer using one of our legacy solutions in their gen one product.

They were moving to a next-gen product where the precision of what they required was far greater. The good news is, as we looked at our Cone Drive technology that they were using originally, we were able to shift them over to cycloidal gearbox through Spinea. That's a little higher cost technology, but much higher precision, which met their need. So that generated a higher value opportunity for us with the same customer. In addition to that, we were able to then convince them to sell them the subsystem instead of just the gearbox, which generated really 2.5, almost three times more revenue than the opportunity would have otherwise.

So we took something that was business at risk and turned it into a much bigger opportunity than it was before, but much more importantly, built credibility with that customer that we actually can provide a solution instead of what we would have done in the past, maybe try to negotiate the price on a technology that really didn't meet their need going forward. It's just an example. When you step to the back of the store operationally, there is even more opportunity there. You go from very simple things like, why would you not buy airline tickets, hotel rooms, and rental cars, and all that one single way? Why would you buy steel two different ways? You wouldn't.

Or how would you manage real estate? You'd manage it all together. That's all kind of table stakes, obvious. Some of that we've already been doing. We're going to do more of it more deliberately. But then how do you take 100 plus operating locations and establish playbooks by archetype? They're not all the same, but they're not all different. Are there four or five different archetypes that you can then establish unique KPIs for those, an automation strategy, and operating those, and then finally sweating those assets? So, the sum of the parts is definitely greater here as we move forward. I'm convinced of that. I'm convinced of that both operationally, but especially in front of the customers.

As we engage with these 80s customers and with our key account plans, we've done a few by now, and wherever we go, we see value. We have to see one yet where we walk home and say, "Well, that was not a good idea." It's working. The early indications are there. Obviously, this takes time. You don't show up the first day and land a bunch of revenue that afternoon. But we do see early wins, we see pipeline, we see orders, we see all the indications that we need to see that give us a lot of confidence that we're headed on the right track.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rob Wertheimer at Melius Research.

Rob Wertheimer: Hi, thanks and good morning.

Rob Wertheimer: I had one kind of in a similar vein, morning, to what David asked. As you've worked through 80/20 and opportunities and things you might cut, is there any other drag in 2027 from fading smaller products that had low volume, et cetera? Then I had a follow-up if I can. Thank you.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Thank you for the question. The short answer is no drag from 80/20 in 2027. We think the drag is behind us, for it was more of an investment. We're now at a point where we're at least paying for that investment through the early actions. I gave some examples in the prepared remarks, and the benefits are starting to flow in as you enter into 2027, where 80/20 is a net benefit. I say that from a cost side, from the cost of implementing 80/20, the cost of training, the cost of all that's a net benefit.

The bigger benefit, obviously, it's called 80/20 and not 20/80 because the benefit doesn't come from the 20s, the benefit comes from the 80s. The benefit comes from growth. That's what's most exciting to me about 80/20, is this engagement with our key customers, key account plans, bringing more than one Timken business to bear to solving a customer problem. That's what will change our trajectory. Frankly, that's what's already helping our Industrial Motion. Our Industrial Motion business now has several quarters in a row where we're growing very nicely in the mid to high single digits. That's expected not only to continue, but to start accelerating that number.

Rob Wertheimer: Perfect. Thank you. Maybe it's small, I don't know, but the electroadhesive acquisition is not one I expected. I wonder if you could expand for a second on how that fits into current either technology or end market. Then does that significantly kind of signal an expansion of your acquisition play field or TAM? I'll stop there. Thank you.

Lucian Boldea: Right. No, look, it's a great question. I have to confess, when it was introduced to me a while back with that name, electroadhesive, I said the same thing. What is mechanical engineering or tribology or precision machining in there? Let me give it a layman's explanation at least that I think of on this technology. Basically think of an e-brake that holds position without consuming electricity. On a humanoid, if it has to pick something up and then it has to hold that position very firmly without really consuming battery life, that's what this technology does. The application, really, humanoid is a great application, but you can think of this as also in other industrial applications.

It's not a brake in the sense of a car, so it doesn't slow something down. It holds position locked. It's either on or off, but it does it in a very energy efficient way. Where battery life is very important, we think this technology is a big enabler, again, in conjunction with actuators, in conjunction with some of the other offerings, because then we'll do the go and we'll do the stop at the same time with equal precision and in an energy efficient manner. That's the idea of the technology. It's part of the overall solution being more of a systems provider.

Operator: Our next question will come from Kyle Menges at Citigroup. Please go ahead.

Kyle Menges: Thanks. Maybe a follow-up on Rob's last question. Lucian, I think you made comments about starting to build up an M&A pipeline, and would just love to hear just anything you can share on maybe how that M&A pipeline is building, areas of focus, and are we still thinking about bolt-ons or could there be potential for anything larger?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Let me start with the last question because that is the easiest one. Yes, still bolt-ons, not something larger. How we think about our M&A pipeline is really way more strategically aligned with the verticals. One of the things that we try to do at Investor Day is to really lay out very, very clearly our roadmap, how we are trying to grow, where we are trying to grow, how we are trying to win. So also the both the where to play and how to win. We articulated the key verticals, and what that means is really we expect our M&A pipeline to really be aligned with those key verticals.

What I will tell you is there would be probably two types of M&A. One, you can think a little bit in terms of the Bijur Delimon being an example. How do I further the technology platforms that I have, continues to solidify my leadership? How do I add more complementary offerings in these key markets that really work with the solutions that we already provide? Then there is a smaller subset which is similar to this investment in this technology, which is R&D make versus buy.

We might do an acquisition that maybe does not have a lot of revenue, but you acquire a technical capability that then you can leverage in the portfolio to bring your current solutions or pull others through the market, but would have to be pretty well aligned with our focus markets and with where we are trying to go. The other part that we are developing and have now developed this playbook of regionally translating our existing acquisitions, that we have 22 of those that we have made in the last 10 years, depending on how exactly, how granular you get with the count, and most of those are regional in Industrial Motion.

So, how we translate those from one region to another will become a playbook for a future M&A as well, where we will be in a great position to buy a single region play that then we can very quickly copy, paste, translate into other regions. That is another avenue to create value with M&A that we now have in place.

Kyle Menges: Got it. That is helpful, Lucian. It seems like since the Investor Day, you continue to talk about 80/20 initiatives and maybe some organizational changes as well, that at least some of which feel somewhat incremental. Would love to just hear what you feel like you have been doing on 80/20 and any other restructuring initiatives that you would say are probably incremental from what you laid out at the Investor Day.

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Look, I think if you polled 19,000 people today, I would bet you won't find many that say it's incremental. We've made a lot of changes in the company. If you think how we were operating a year ago, we had an Engineered Bearings segment that was running like a vertical P&L, and then Industrial Motion running separately. We've turned that basically 90 degrees on its side. We have a single Chief Operating Officer that runs a single customer-facing organization that's regional first, but inside those regions, it's verticalized. It's not territories, it's not product lines, it's verticals, it's industries.

The entire sales force went from, you had an EB sales force, and then you had a dozen IM sales forces. Now you have a Timken sales force. If you go to Europe, you have a Timken sales force that might be focused on automation, you might have one that's focused on aerospace and defense, and they're specialized in that area. That transformation on the customer-facing side is dramatic. We have a technology organization under a Chief Technology Officer that now includes the entire company. It's not independent organizations inside the P&L, so that's pulled together. On the operations side, we have a single COO that includes bearings, includes Industrial Motion.

Inside the P&Ls, we used to have the P&Ls aligned by market. They're now aligned with the factories. We would have a rail P&L in bearings and aerospace one. Now, they'll share the factory. By the way, that's no longer the case. I have a small bore and a large bore P&L ownership in bearings that basically is aligned with a network of factories that then can be leveraged so they can sweat the assets. There's been very significant changes under the surface to really operationalize this. The more significant change, and Steve Ribaudo is driving even more of that, as he joined our COO, is that's the hardware, the org structure.

The software obviously is the operating model, that discipline, that cadence. We now have a cadence every month. We call it business decision week. That's where it's a prescribed agenda. It happens the same day every month. It's the same system. It's the same reporting, just new numbers every month. We refer to what did we do, what did we say we were going to do, did we get it done, what are we doing to mitigate? All that is very transparent, very prescribed.

There's a substantial amount of operationalizing the strategy that's happened, some before Investor Day, but most of it after Investor Day, and it's now really taking shape on the back of the store with Steve Ribaudo joining in September as COO.

Kyle Menges: Great. That is helpful. I guess this was all kind of within that plan that you shared at the Investor Day?

Lucian Boldea: Yes. It is within the plan, but some of it, that Investor Day was a plan. It is now past tense actions.

Kyle Menges: Got it. That is helpful. Thank you.

Operator: Our next question will come from Steve Barger at KeyBanc.

Steve Barger: Hey, thanks. Really nice to see the positive backlog trend. How much of the mid-single-digit backlog growth is OEM versus aftermarket and distribution, and where are you seeing the most acceleration in OEM schedules?

Mike Discenza: Yeah. Hey, Steve, Mike here. Thanks for the question. I will come at that question a slightly different way, because we don't really classify the backlog by channel. What I would say is that our channel partners, we feel confident that the inventory levels are at a good place. So, the backlog is commensurate with kind of the sell-through rate, if you will. So, in order intake, strong there, commensurate with strong sales growth. on the OE side, Lucian Boldea referred to where we are seeing the strength, but maybe to get one level more specific, we saw strong order book growth in our infrastructure market, which would include things like heavy industries, off-highway, et cetera.

Of course, aerospace has been growing strong and continued to grow strong, and that's in both segments, both Industrial Motion and Engineered Bearings, see continued backlog growth there. General industrial, which again cuts across a lot of the lighter, say, industrial markets. The one place where we obviously are struggling from an order book standpoint was wind energy, which was down substantially, and we already said would be down again in the fourth quarter. So, hopefully that helps give a little color.

Steve Barger: Yeah, I appreciate that. Lucian, you said that early minimum order and customer segmentation actions are improving profitability without affecting revenue. Are the benefits that you're seeing so far from a better price versus cost to serve, or are you already driving incremental growth and share of wallet with the high-priority customers?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Both are already happening. I think that we have a few examples now with larger customers where really probably September was the first month where I could really hang my hat on a significant number that made a difference to say, "Okay, yes, this is starting to pay off." I can identify discrete opportunities at these large customers that were directly related to opportunities we got through a different level of engagement. I think that started really in earnest in September, and then as we expand that effort, I'm optimistic, obviously, that's going to grow not only with the customers we've already engaged, but also as we expand the customers.

The minimum order value that came from, when you do 80/20, you do a zero-up, and you kind of look in the mirror and say, "Okay, what does it actually cost me to process an order?" It's not a small number. Then you realize that maybe you were processing orders that were below the revenue that it costs you to process the order, and why on earth would you do that? Also recognizing that, by the way, the customer that places the order, it's not free for them either to place that order, and it just doesn't make any sense. We have a minimum order value now that's going to allow us to be more efficient.

We will, for the time being, what that does in the immediate term is it frees up the resources to serve those 80s customers better, because obviously when we engage with those 80 customers and we say, "We need more from you," that means we will do more for them. We will give them better service, we will give them better lead times, we will give them better visibility, and as a result, they will give us more of their share of wallet, but that requires people as well. That's that redeployment of fewer orders to process because there's fewer smaller ones, more time for the big customers.

But as we continue to do this, there will be some productivity opportunities. Obviously, there will be a net benefit from a margin standpoint.

Mike Discenza: Yeah, and maybe Steve, just a reminder of what we have said all along, which was 80/20, the first half was a drag on the company. The second half, which we are squarely in right now, those benefits are really offsetting some of those costs. Then we will expect to see that drop-through on the margin really as we get into 2027. We spent the last almost a year now, we have been doing this for a little less than a year, doing a lot of learnings, and Lucian Boldea has referenced several of the tools that we have put in place. There are many tools. Each business, as we have segmented, has different needs.

So, a lot of activity going on there, deploying the tools, then looking for that to start delivering results next year, both top and bottom line in a meaningful way.

Operator: Next, we will hear from the line of Tim Thein, or Thein rather, at Raymond James. I hope I said your name correctly, sir. Please go ahead.

Tim Thein: Yeah, that was a good effort. Yeah, just on a question is on kind of the visibility you have for 2027. Some of your longer cycle business or longer cycle, larger backlog-based businesses that you called out earlier is driving a lot of the kind of the order momentum. So, A&D and as well as automation and robotics. I mean, it is nearly 40% of revenue. So, just as you kind of exit the year, I am just curious if you could speak to where you expect to exit the year.

Kind of how much of that mid-single-digit growth, again, and nothing is certain, but just kind of how much of that is kind of already within your control, just based on what you would expect to exit the year in terms of having that in backlog?

Lucian Boldea: Yeah, Tim. So, look, it's always a little bit difficult to link pipeline in long-cycle business to revenue in a short period of time, especially in the near term. With that caveat, in the long run, it does all flow through and all even out. So, when I step back and look at the aerospace and defense business, for example, where does the pipeline sit? Again, I mentioned Q3 of 2026 versus Q3 of 2025, a significant double-digit increase. Same with automation and robotics, dramatic double-digit increase. When I look at the revenue side of both of these verticals, whether it's Q3, whether it's Q4, again, very, very strong performance.

Aerospace and defense, we've made the investments in manufacturing that have been a drag on us on cost. But I'm happy to share with you that our revenues are up double digits in aerospace and defense on the bearing side. As I look at Industrial Motion, it's basically a 20% year-over-year kind of trajectory. The pipeline is growing more than that. I'm still, unfortunately or fortunately, still building past dues and backlog in spite of our best efforts. The extra revenue, especially on the bearing side in aerospace, only came on the back of us being able to produce more because we were capacity limited. So, those investments are starting to pay off.

We have other step changes in the ability to serve that are coming in aerospace where we've invested in more infrastructure, more material. So far, what we're getting is a bit of try harder with more people. We've hired more people, and some of the equipment we invested in, that's coming now and will help us. There are a number of things then on the defense side, especially on the marine side. We have a number of pretty significant projects, to your point, on long cycle that we will have to deliver actually fairly, start delivering, start working on them, and have revenue recognition in 2027 from those. Those are pretty significant. We feel very good about winning these opportunities.

We're in the final stages of bidding. We obviously have a very motivated customer who wants to move with speed, and that will further help us on the defense side. Again, the pivot we're making, we feel very good about. I just want everybody to recognize we're managing to a net number. It's the undercurrent of we're exiting a market, we're doing divestitures, we're doing growth at the same time. What we said we're doing, what we said we're working on is working. It's working very well.

The early indicators are very positive that we're headed on the right track, and that's why we're sitting here earlier than normal, reaffirming our views on 2027 without doing a firm guide, but getting as close as we can to that.

Mike Discenza: The other thing just in our control and that we've communicated is pricing. We said we included 100 basis points of pricing in our long-term targets and expect to be able to deliver on that promise as well. We have that in our control to help with that growth.

Tim Thein: Got it. Okay. Mike, one quick one on that. There was an earlier question on the mix impact in the quarter. Curious if you dovetail. Usually when I think of mix, I think of the distribution playing an important role in that calculation. How did distribution fare in the quarter and what you're expecting in the fourth quarter in terms of global distribution sales?

Mike Discenza: Yeah. Distribution was not a significant impact on that mix. It really was a little bit more of the, as Lucian Boldea referred to, the regional impact, Europe being down. Of course, some of our acquisitions, Industrial Motion, heavier in Europe, so mix from that. When I think about distribution going forward, like I said, we feel that inventory is at a good place. Our big customers that have announced their growth rates, we feel comfortable that we'll be able to match those. We look for continued growth in those markets. Of course, when that grows, it does help with mix. But in the quarter, it wasn't a contributor to the negative mix.

Operator: Next, we will hear from the line of Tomo Sano at JPMorgan.

Tomo Sano: Thank you. It was encouraging to see how One Timken emphasized at the recent trade shows. As you continue to implement 80/20 and One Timken, how are you positioning Timken in emerging areas like humanoid robotics? Are you bringing capabilities across the brands together to customize higher-margin solutions, and how does that fit with your strategic priorities?

Lucian Boldea: Yes. Thank you for the question. So, especially if I start to where we sit today on the robotic side, because humanoid is more forward-looking, but on the humanoid side, we're already doing that. So we've put together a platform, a precision drive platform. So this constitutes our Cone Drive business, our Spinea business, and our CGI business that we've acquired. So those three are kind of the tip of the spear of the One Timken. Obviously, behind them, very close behind, is our linear motion business, our automatic lubrication systems business, and then our bearings businesses.

But the tip of the spear is that platform, that precision drive, that really is meant to go engage with the OEMs, because you want to bring that credibility together to be a solution provider, and the only way you do that is you come with multiple solutions. You don't want to come with the full toolkit that maybe some of it is not relevant. You want to come with enough in your prototyping.

How it fits with the strategy, both on robotics and on the humanoids, is to really go to these subsystems, to where instead of selling just an actuator, and there's plenty of revenue to be made in a humanoid or a robot with actuators, but instead of just the actuator, might have the gearbox, you might have the frameless motor attached to it, you might have other subsystem. But really, it's looking at that sub-component. It's not making the humanoid, but maybe you're looking at the wrist, maybe you're looking at an ankle, that type of approach.

If you're thinking of a robotic arm, you might make the components in the robotic arm, but also the robot transfer unit that comes out of our linear motion business that is linked to that. So that's how we try to think about that, is really solve the unique customer problem, which is why we're more excited about industrial robotics, frankly speaking, than humanoids. Humanoids might be a little more mass-produced. Industrial robotics, as you alluded to, is way more bespoke. There will be an in-between there, which is the industrial high-performance humanoid. That is also of great interest for professional humanoid.

That would be interesting for us as well as an opportunity, and we're working with OEMs there in prototyping, in development. Already, we have programs I should have started with. We now have a center of excellence around humanoids. We have a cross-functional team that's up and running, that's engaging with these OEMs, that's really looking at the technologies across the company and we're not relying on one P&L at a time to engage with customers.

Chris Dankert: Hey, good morning. Peter on for Chris today.

Chris Dankert: Just going back quickly to here on 80/20. I know we've previously been given the target of, I think, 75% of initiatives being rolled out by Q3. Lucian Boldea: Yeah. Maybe clarify a little bit. We did 80/20 with an 80/20 mindset, so we started there.

Yes, it is fully underway. It is operationalized. There's an operating system that goes with it. There's a review cadence that goes with it that Mike and I both personally sit in on a high level of frequency and check in with the teams across all these work streams. They all now have dashboards, KPIs, milestones, all the things that you can imagine, and that is all underway. Everybody trained, and the work stream's fully operationalized. It's all moving forward.

Chris Dankert: Perfect. I appreciate it. I'll pass it back.

Neil Frohnapple: Thank you, operator, and thank you everyone for joining us today. If you have any further questions after today's call, please contact me. Thank you, and this concludes our call.

#3192. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3189. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3187. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3185. Navios Maritime (NMM) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Higher charter rates and debt reduction shaped the quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Navios Maritime Partners L.P. (NMM -1.68%) reported increased net income for the third quarter as the company utilized cash flow for fleet expansion and debt reduction. Management emphasized the visibility provided by its multisegment charter backlog and progress toward long-term leverage targets. The company continued its strategy of fleet renewal by committing to newbuilding vessels while returning capital to unitholders through repurchases and cash distributions. Chief Trading Officer Vandewalle noted that geopolitical disruptions, including the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have tightened global tanker availability and influenced freight rates across all vessel segments.

Operator: Thank you for joining us for Navios Maritime Partners Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. This conference call could contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 about Navios Partners. Navios Partners does not assume any obligation to update this information contained in this conference call. The agenda for today's call is as follows: First, Ms.

Frangou will offer opening remarks. Next, Mr. Desypris will give an overview of Navios Partners segment data. Next, Mrs. Tsironi will give an overview of Navios Partners' financial results. Then Mr. Vandewalle will provide an industry overview. And lastly, we'll open the call to take questions. Now I turn the call over to Navios Partners Chairwoman and CEO, Ms. Angeliki Frangou. Angeliki?

Angeliki Frangou: Good morning, and thank you all for joining us on today's call. For the third quarter, we reported net income of $185.7 million and earnings per common unit of $6.42. For the first 9 months, we reported net income of $460 million and earnings per common unit of $15.83. We also announced a cash distribution per unit for the quarter of $0.06. We continue to operate in a complex global environment characterized by geopolitical uncertainty, conflict and changing trade patterns. Our performance demonstrates the strength of our diversified business and the benefits of our disciplined approach to capital allocation and risk management. During the third quarter, Navios used its strong cash flow to add vessels to its fleet.

We made an investment of over $700 million to acquire 7 newbuilding vessels: 4 container ships, which were chartered out for about $400 million in revenue, and 3 newbuilding tankers, which are subject to ongoing discussion for charters of 5 years or longer. In addition, we accelerated the repayment of $90 million of debt maturing from 2028 through 2030. Turning to Slide 3. Our fleet has an average age of 8.5 years compared with an industry average of 13.8 years. Our tanker fleet, with an average age of 4.9 years, is particularly young compared with the industry tanker average of 14.2 years.

We believe the youth of our fleet provides a competitive advantage through, among other things, lower operating costs, better fuel efficiency and stronger charter preference. Please turn to Slide 4. Navios is a leading maritime transportation company, owning and operating a modern fleet of 182 vessels across 3 segments and 15 asset classes. Our in-the-water fleet is split into thirds, with about 1/3 of the value in each of the tanker, dry bulk and container segments. Overall, this fleet is valued at approximately $8.7 billion with $6.2 billion in vessel net equity value. Our fully delivered fleet has an estimated charter-free value of approximately $12.4 billion.

We have contracted revenue backlog of approximately $5 billion, providing significant visibility into future earnings and importantly, providing coverage past 2030. At the quarter end, we had a net LTV of 23.1%. Our balance sheet is strong with $657 million available liquidity and credit ratings of Ba3 from Moody's and BB from S&P. Please turn to Slide 5. We maintain a disciplined risk management culture, continuously monitoring and assessing our exposure, diligently evaluating and structuring transactions and maintaining robust insurance coverage, particularly important in a war-risk environment. Our focus is on building a business capable of generating value across multiple market cycles. We couple this culture with diversification and, together, our platform provides optionality across markets..

Please turn to Slide 6, where we outline our recent developments. I previously mentioned that Navios had net income of $185.7 million or $6.42 earnings per common unit during the third quarter. As to our balance sheet, approximately 44% of our debt is fixed interest rates, providing protection against interest rate volatility, while 52% of our debt has no loan-to-value covenant. Our debt maturity profile is staggered, limiting near-term refinancing pressure, and we have 62 debt-free vessels worth around $2.4 billion. During Q3 and through the fourth quarter to date, we committed approximately $703 million to the acquisition of 7 newbuilding vessels. These acquisitions included four 10,100 TEU container ships, one VLCC and two MR2 product tankers.

We also entered into a long-term contract for $735 million. In addition, we agreed to sell a 17-year-old capesize vessel for $30.8 million. We continue to replace older assets with modern vessels while seeking to secure attractive employment. Please turn to Slide 7, where we address our return of capital. We authorized an additional $200 million common unit repurchase program in 2026. Since the program commenced in the second quarter of 2024, we repurchased approximately 2 million common units for a total consideration of $104.4 million. This reduced outstanding common units by 6.7% from approximately 30.2 million to 28.2 million. These repurchases are particularly attractive when our units trade at a meaningful discount to the underlying asset value.

The average analyst estimate to our net asset value is at approximately $187 per unit. Thus, repurchases since 2024 have generated approximately $202 million in estimated net asset value accretion equivalent to $6.90 per unit. Over the last 12 months, we have returned approximately $48 million to unitholders through repurchases and cash distributions. In allocating capital to a unit repurchase program, we consider the relative attractiveness of alternative uses of capital, including the availability of investments that can enhance long-term cash flow generation, the preservation of liquidity, maintaining prudent leverage and safeguarding balance sheet strength. Please turn to Slide 8, where we review Navios' track records over the past 5 years. We are focused on building a platform of excellence. Adjusted net income for the first 9 months of '26 doubled to $396 million compared to $196 million for the same period in '25.

Adjusted earnings and earnings per common unit for the first 9 months of '26 were $13.6 and $15.8, respectively. Turning to Slide 14. I will briefly discuss some key balance sheet data. Long-term borrowings, including the current portion and the senior secured bond net of deferred fees, increased by $87 million to $2.25 billion following the delivery of 8 newbuildings during the first 9 months of the year.
