In addition, 44% of our debt is fixed at an average interest rate of 6.3%, while 52% carries no loan-to-value covenant. We have also partially mitigated higher interest rate costs by lowering the average margin on our floating rate debt and bareboat liabilities for the in the water fleet to 1.7%. I would like to note that the average margin for the committed floating rate debt of our newbuilding program is 1.4%.

I'll now pass the call to Vincent Vandewalle, Navios Partners' Chief Trading Officer, to take you through the industry section. Vincent?

Vincent Vandewalle: Thank you, Eri. Strait of Hormuz closure has created a major energy and shipping shock, affecting about 20% of the worldwide crude product and LNG flows. The disruption has tightened tanker availability and driven freight rates for all sizes sharply higher. Rates for VLCCs hit all-time highs, reaching $1.4 million per day and remained elevated even as all flows out of the Middle East returned to pre-war levels. Increased crude volumes from the U.S.A., Brazil, Venezuela and Guyana heading to both Europe and Asia are adding more ton miles as worldwide stocks have been drawn down and oil demand continues at high levels.

Product tanker rates have also risen with the Baltic Clean Tanker Index reaching an all-time high of 3,015 points last week, 264% higher than long-term average of 826. Higher fuel costs and security of supply concern continue to drive the purchasing and transportation of commodities and finished goods. This has raised rates for dry bulk assets for both Capes and Panamaxes and has continued to support container time charter rates. The conflict in Ukraine and effects due to El Nino will also add ton miles for most vessel types. We expect coal imports to continue at elevated levels, while LNG passage through Hormuz remains restricted.

With negotiations between the U.S. and Iran at an impasse and increasing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Southern Red Sea, vessel utilization will continue to run at high levels, supporting elevated rates for the near term. Medium-term trade adjustments depend on how long oil prices stay elevated. And, for example, whether decreased fertilizer availability affects crop supply later this year. Strategic and commercial crude and product reserves will need to be restocked, which should keep tanker rates elevated over the longer term. However, prolonged Hormuz closure could still trigger a global slowdown or a recessionary demand shock, which could affect all shipping markets. Please turn to Slide 18 for the review of the dry bulk industry.

Demand growth for dry bulk trade has been relatively stable over the last 25 years at about 4% compound annual ton-mile growth. The current order book stands at about 15% of the total fleet and is expected to remain low due to high newbuilding prices, uncertainty about new fuel regulations, yard availability and general market outlook. The fleet is aging quickly with 39% of the vessels 15 years old. With older vessels far exceeding those on order, supply should be constrained over the medium term. Please turn to Slide 19. The main driver of dry bulk demand will be strong Atlantic Basin iron ore growth over the next several years with new projects in Guinea, Brazil and Liberia.

The largest new project is Simandou in Guinea, which started shipments at the end of last year and is expected to ramp up to 120 million by '28. Mid-October year-to-date shipments were about 20 million long-haul tons from 0 last year. Vale in Brazil has three new projects totaling 50 million tonnes expected to start exporting by the end of '26 and Liberia will add 10 million tonnes of exports in '26. Other African iron ore exports projects have been announced, but awaiting final investment decisions. In total, these 180 million tonnes are all long-haul ton miles trading, creating demand for an additional 249 Capes.

With the current order book of only 228 Capes due by '28, a further tightening of supply and demand is expected over the next few years, benefiting rates. Overall, the dry bulk market looks positive based on steady long-term demand growth and a constrained supply of vessels. Please turn to Slide 21 for the review of the tanker industry. As to supply, we see a tanker order book of 26%, about 50% of the fleet is already over 15 years old, rising quickly in the next few years. With older vessels exceeding the order book and yards offering first deliveries in '29 or '30, supply is set to be tight for several years. Please turn to Slide 22.

VLCCs reached record spot earnings of $1.4 million a day recently as a portion of the fleet has been sanctioned, damaged, restricted in trading or dedicated to ship-to-ship shuttle service through Hormuz. In all, 28% of the VLCC fleet has been restricted from normal operations, leading to exceptional spot and long-term charter rates. Please turn to Slide 23. Middle East crude oil flows have recently returned to pre-war levels, although their composition has shifted significantly. Increasing use of ship-to-ship transfers, along with exports out of the Red Sea and via pipelines have created more inefficiencies and led VLCC rates to the current extreme elevated rates. This has also helped Suezmax and Aframax crude tanker rates to rise across the board.

The tanker market also looks positive over the medium term based on a low order book compared with an aging and reduced fleet due to sanctions. Please turn to Slide 25 for the review of the container industry. After the COVID pandemic, containership orders were mainly for the biggest units with fleet expansion in large vessels set to continue at a high level. Currently, 73% of the order book is for ships with 9,000 TEU capacity or greater and only 23% of the order book is for 2,000 to 9,000 TEU capacity where Navios is most active. Note that by '29, more than 50% of the 2,000 to 9,000 TEU fleet will be 20 years or older.

Small segments of the fleet are well positioned to take advantage of shifting trading patterns. As shown on the right-hand graph, growth in non-mainlane trades generally exceed the traditional mainlane trades to the U.S. and Europe due to tariffs and higher growth in developing economies, notwithstanding Iran war-related dislocations this year. Trades involving the Southern Hemisphere, mostly served by smaller-sized vessels, are expected to see continued healthy growth as this trade shift continues. Overall, Navios Fleet is well positioned within the container market and continues to benefit from long-term employment with our high-quality charters. This concludes our presentation. I would now like to turn the call over to Angeliki Frangou for her final comments. Angeliki?

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you, Vincent. This concludes our formal presentation. We open the call to questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And we'll take our first question from Omar Nokta with Clarksons Securities.

Omar Nokta: Clearly, you have very strong results and you continue to reinvest in the business, divesting older vessels, acquiring newbuildings primarily with long-term charters. I think, obviously, a real significant thing that's developed here recently is at least one of the many things has been the reduction in your net LTV. You've gotten it down to 23%. That's your long-term target of trying to get it to that 20% to 25% range. So congratulations on that. So I guess now that you're here, is there anything that changes the business approach? Your market footprint has generally stayed the same within the three main aspects of your business. But does anything change from here? Do you look to be more acquisitive?

Is there a target you want to keep through the cycles with this net LTV? Yes, any color you can give on anything that changes from here based on you reaching your target?

Angeliki Frangou: Number one, I'll say the target is one thing, but also you can see that we care about return to our investors. As you know, I'm a 20% owner of the -- almost 20% owner of the equity. So we are fully aligned here. Important thing is you have to see what we have done with our cash this year. In 2026, we spent about four, $450 million cash for newbuildings. We prepaid in order to reach our LTV numbers about $170 million accelerated debt repayment. And we returned so far about $40 million return of capital to our investors, $660 million up to now.

As we are -- the year is finishing in Q1, we will recalibrate our return of capital and seeing the conditions at the time. But one thing we have done is we built NAV and also by pushing NAV, we get a share price to chase this NAV.

Omar Nokta: Angeliki, no, that's good context. And so we'll stay tuned on things as they develop. And maybe just kind of as a follow-up, you've had this long-term exposure to the three main segments of shipping of tankers, containers, dry bulk. And you obviously invested within all three and recycled proceeds into new ships in those markets. But as you kind of think about where things are, I know there's a lot to think about, you have plenty of flexibility. But do you see investment opportunities for Navios outside these three core areas within shipping perhaps or any other segments that look interesting from an investment standpoint?

Angeliki Frangou: Listen, the beauty of our platform is that we are able to take advantage of any market. And this is what it makes it unique. And I think this is something that we like to stress. I mean it allows. We have $1 billion in platform on EBITDA generation LTM. We have a very low leverage. And we have the ability and we have been expanding and building NAV while we are deleveraging. So that platform -- and we have a contracted revenue of about $5 billion that allow us to have contracted revenue beyond 2030.

So this kind of a platform allows you to be able to be opportunistic on the -- on what we see as an area to expand. And one thing I want to say, we are very mindful of our investors. Think about we completed $100 million of a buyback, and we have already announced a $200 million buyback. What we have done, you have to see it over a period of time. We have -- over the last 5 years, we more than doubled our NAV. So we are chasing. This is our success. We are building that NAV. On the same time, we have done -- we have grown -- our share price has increased over 300%.

So this is not one quarter, not one year. It's multiple years of effort to provide results.

Omar Nokta: Indeed, we can see it. So well done. Congratulations on the latest, and we'll see how things develop from here.

Operator: We'll move next to Stephanie Moore with Jefferies.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: I guess just as you think about your Q4 VLCC days are fixed at just over, I think, 70%. How are you thinking about spot versus term coverage from here? I would love to hear your thoughts just given where we are in the market and then appetite as we think about more days are open into 2027.

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you. This is a good question. The nature of our platform allows us to have flexibility. So this depends on the sector and part of the cycle. So, you will see that the contracted revenue allows us to be totally non-biased on where we take the exposure. If you see for this year and Stratos had analyzed very well is we have a lot of exposure on our dry bulk capesize vessels. We see an opportunity here and why we keep larger vessels on the tanker segment, VLCC exposure. So we are opportunistic on where we see the exposure.

On the container side, on the other side, we see the nice cash flows as a good bedrock for our visibility.

Efstratios Desypris: Just one quick add-on here, Stephanie, on the exposure that we have on the tankers. -- as Angeliki said we have covered -- we have a lot of contracted revenue on the tanker side, about $2.4 billion of contracted revenue. But what we have opened is about 1/3 of our days, which are open for next year. And basically, you will see that these are mostly the VLs that are on spot exposure because there, we see the bigger volatility and the bigger upside. And again, if we also drill down on the other sectors on the dry bulk, where you do not have a lot of very healthy contract -- long-term contracted revenue.

Now we see the market picking up and we see availability of longer contracts. You see that the exposure there is mostly for next year is about 90% and the vast majority of it is on capesize. And containers, of course, as Angeliki said, I mean, we are almost fully fixed for next year because there, we capitalize on a very strong market.

Stephanie Benjamin Moore: Really helpful. And then just as a follow-up, you booked, I think, over $63 million of sale gains year-to-date. And as I think look at tanker values here that are up well over 40%. Maybe with your vessels that are over 15 years old, should we expect asset sales to be up into 2027? Or how should we think about overall sale potential there?

Angeliki Frangou: I think, Stephanie, you have seen we are very opportunistic on that. Earlier in the year, we sold VLCCs that were 17 years old. Today's environment, you are actually generating -- in a month you're generating such numbers that don't make sense; you're making multiples of the value. So it depends on the situation. Where we see value, we will automatically do it. And we have been very -- this is a continuous process. So I cannot tell you the moment. It depends on the market versus chartering, which we are very disciplined and we will always do. And even if the chartering opportunity to the market value of the vessel may be equal, we will sell one, keep one.

We have this continuous program. And we have done that. We have sold over $1 billion almost $1.2 billion on vessels. This is a continuous effort.

Operator: And this does conclude the question-and-answer portion of today's event. I would now like to hand the call back to Angeliki for any additional or closing remarks.

Angeliki Frangou: Thank you. This completes our Q3 results. Thank you.

Apple has a MacBook Neo 2 planned for early 2027, per Mark Gurman, and a new report from Digitimes indicates the company is expecting it to be a massive hit.

When the MacBook Neo debuted earlier this year, it became an instant hit.

Driven primarily by MacBook Neo, Apple set a new record for its best ever sales week among first-time Mac buyers.

But as popular as the first MacBook Neo has proven, it sounds like Apple is planning for its successor to be an even bigger hit.

Apple has given suppliers a shipment forecast of 16 million MacBook Neo units for 2027, about double the nearly 8 million units expected in 2026, according to supply-chain sources.

16 million units for 2027 is a huge increase from MacBook Neo’s 2026 numbers.

A small portion of that increase can be attributed to the MacBook Neo being on sale for longer in 2027. The original Neo arrived in March 2026, so 2027 will have the advantage of January and February sales.

It will be wildly popular bc it will be the only MacBook any one can afford.

With reporting pointing to a MacBook Neo 2 launching in early 2027, it sounds like Apple is confident the Neo will prove even more popular in the year ahead.

#3182. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3181. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

#3178. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.
